entries.term: Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue
entries.note: [[see:Francis Grose]]'s 1785 dictionary of street slang and cant, gathered from ordinary speakers rather than literature, expanded in 1811 and prefaced with apologies for its rudeness.
His more prudish dictionary left out indecent words and used only literary citations, unlike the [[see:Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue]].
From Latin [[from:vulgaris]], of the common people; it once meant common or ordinary rather than crude.
Like [[see:vulgar]], once meant something ordinary before turning negative.
Once simply meant raw or basic, another word that shifted like [[see:vulgar]].
Once meant a non-gentry person before turning negative, like [[see:vulgar]].
Military man, illustrator and antiquarian who compiled his dictionary from night-time street talk; very fat, he joked about his name, and [[see:Robert Burns]] teased him about it.
[[see:Francis Grose]]'s friend, who went out with him at night collecting street speech; the hosts joke about his name.
[[see:Francis Grose]]'s first book, a heavily illustrated popular guide to architectural sites from the 1770s.
The Scottish poet befriended [[see:Francis Grose]] in Scotland and wrote verses mocking his size, including a deathbed epigram.
Military slang for small beer, five pints of which a landlord was once legally obliged to give each soldier free.
A drunk who vomits into the lap of the person sitting opposite.
Taking away the front door, a method Kent Street landlords used on tenants more than a fortnight behind with the rent.
Grose's term for eggs; [[see:Polari]] speakers later also called eggs cackle farts.

entries.term: hoddy doddy, all arse and no body
entries.note: A phrase for a short, clumsy person of either sex.
A pimple or carbuncle on the face from drinking, such as a swollen red nose, in 18th-century London slang.
A valet or footman, so called because they walk behind their master or mistress.
An insulting term for a drummer.
An insulting term for a fiddler.
A constable, said this way to avoid a first syllable that sounds like the indecent [[see:monosyllable]].
A schoolmaster, probably a play on [[see:phlebotomist]], suggesting indecency like [[see:bum brusher]].
Another of Grose's terms for a schoolmaster, accusing them of indecency.
Grose's entry 'bothered or both-eared': talked to in both ears at once and confused, apparently a folk etymology of [[see:bother]].
Ultimately from an Irish word meaning to deafen, close in spirit to the folk etymology [[see:both-eared]].
Tying a lantern to a hobbled horse so it looks like a ship's light at night, luring ships ashore to wreck and plunder them.
A cheat drops money, 'finds' it in front of a country lad, then lures him to the pub to rob him.

entries.term: A Caveat or Warning for Common Cursitors
entries.note: [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s 1567 exposé of vagabonds, with a taxonomy of rogues and a cant glossary that ended up in Grose's dictionary.
Means runner; used in the title of [[see:A Caveat or Warning for Common Cursitors]] for vagabonds.
A landowner who collected criminal cant to expose vagabonds, and cruelly had [[see:Nicholas Blunt]] chased, arrested, whipped and imprisoned.
Senior professional rogues in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy.
Rogues who were former soldiers, in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy.
A horse thief in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy of rogues.
Female rogues in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy, alongside [[see:morts]].
Female rogues in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy, alongside [[see:doxies]].
Female peddlers in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy.
Rogues who pretended to be mute, in [[see:Thomas Harman]]'s taxonomy.
Rogues Harman said faked epilepsy to trick people; he accused [[see:Nicholas Blunt]] of this.
Alias Nicholas Jennings, a mentally ill man [[see:Thomas Harman]] branded a counterfeit crank, later recognised and had whipped, pilloried and imprisoned.
In-group jargon of a particular group; perhaps from Latin [[from?:cantus]], song, via mockery of friars' chanting, and perhaps influenced by Gaelic words for speech.
A specialised jargon meant to set an in-group apart from outsiders, used to define [[see:cant]].
The modern term for speech specific to certain groups, covering [[see:cant]] and [[see:argot]].
A coded variety of a language with standard grammar but keywords swapped in a patterned way; narrower than [[see:cant]].

entries.term: Dictionnaire comique, satyrique, critique, burlesque, libre et proverbial
entries.translation: comic, satirical, critical, burlesque, free and proverbial dictionary
entries.note: [[see:Philippe-Joseph Le Roux]]'s dictionary of Parisian underworld terms, credited by Grose as the model for his own.
The Frenchman who compiled the [[see:Dictionnaire comique, satyrique, critique, burlesque, libre et proverbial]].
A word for testicles Rob found in Le Roux's dictionary and had to check with his wife.
A verb in Le Roux's dictionary for which, the hosts say, English has no straightforward equivalent.
Grose's euphemism for the C-word, used to avoid indecency; the word itself is covered in their swear-word episode.
One of Grose's terms for a woman's bosom.
One of Grose's terms for breasts.
One of Grose's terms for breasts.
One of Grose's terms relating to breasts.
Breasts, as in 'she sported her dairy', meaning she pulled out her breast.
Jess's favourite: the place 'where Adam made his first entry'.
Grose's usual word, besides the [[see:monosyllable]], for a woman's genitals.
One of Grose's terms for a woman's [[see:commodity]].
One of Grose's terms for a woman's [[see:commodity]].
One of Grose's terms for a woman's [[see:commodity]].
One of Grose's terms for a woman's [[see:commodity]].
Also Miss Brown; a term for a woman's [[see:commodity]] that Grose doesn't explain.
From a popular song with the refrain 'her black joke and belly so white'; figuratively the [[see:monosyllable]].
A term for the [[see:monosyllable]], after [[see:Matthew Buckinger]], born without hands or legs, who married a tall, handsome woman.
Born without hands and legs, he drew coats of arms, toured showing himself for money, and gave his name to [[see:Buckinger's boot]].
A large, relaxed penis; also a dull or lifeless fellow.
A man whose scrotum hangs longer than his penis, 'whose shot pouch is larger than the barrel of his piece'.
Another word for a schoolmaster with a second, ruder sense that Jess leaves unsaid.
Listed as the copulation of foxes, then used in a cant sense for that of men and women.
Already discussed before; first found in a 1400s-era poem as a nonsense refrain, and Grose claims it evokes [[from?:diletto]], a woman's delight.

entries.term: box the Jesuit and get cockroaches
entries.note: A cant term for masturbation, a crime said to be 'much practised by the reverend fathers of that society'.
Lying one on top of the other, like slices of bread, as with 'John and his maid'.
To lie with a woman on the floor; groundsils are a building's foundations, so panting breath is exhaled at ground level.
One of the sex words found in Grose's dictionary.
One of the sex words found in Grose's dictionary.
One of the sex words found in Grose's dictionary.
To copulate or to beat, meant as an onomatopoeic sound of copulation rather than an acronym; reminiscent of the song [[see:WAP (song)]].
A fairly famous recent song with an acronym title, recalled by Grose's [[see:wap]].
Grose's name for Ireland, because it rains so much.
A mocking name for Scotland in Grose's dictionary, alongside [[see:Scratchland]].
A mocking name for Scotland in Grose's dictionary, alongside [[see:Itchland]].
Grose defines it as a she-dog and 'the most offensive appellation that can be given to an English woman'.
A word for an effeminate-looking fellow, silly now but probably nasty then.
A shabby, ill-dressed fellow.
Used ironically, as in 'I will anoint you with the oil of gladness', meaning I will beat you.

entries.term: A Dictionary of Modern Slang, Cant, and Vulgar Words
entries.note: [[see:John Camden Hotten]]'s 1859 dictionary, published anonymously by 'a London antiquary', with large sections on back slang and rhyming slang.
He published his slang dictionary anonymously, perhaps to divert attention from the erotica he also published anonymously.
Well documented in Hotten's dictionary, with examples like [[see:artful dodger]] and [[see:round the houses]]; bits of it are found in [[see:Polari]].
Rhyming slang for a shilling.
Rhyming slang for a coat.
Rhyming slang for a lodger.
Rhyming slang for going to sleep.
Rhyming slang for the eyes, like [[see:mince pies]].
Rhyming slang for the eyes, like [[see:puddings and pies]].
Rhyming slang for to fight.
Rhyming slang for trousers, rhyming with a vulgar, meaning common, pronunciation of the word.
Rhyming slang for a shilling, rhyming with the common pronunciation 'shillin'.
London gay slang used while homosexuality was illegal, from [[from:Parlyaree]] with bits of rhyming slang, Italian, Yiddish and Latin; now revived.
Theatrical or circus slang, sometimes also called Polari, which the gay community adopted to form [[gave:Polari]].
Painfully uncool; first recorded in [[see:Polari]], in a [[see:Round the Horne]] script about 'naff gnomes', and not an acronym for 'not available for fucking'.
Radio show whose sketches with [[see:Julian and Sandy]] give the earliest written citation of [[see:naff]].
Famous star of [[see:Round the Horne]] who played Sandy.
Two gay characters in [[see:Round the Horne]] sketches whose dialogue first records [[see:naff]].
Played Julian opposite [[see:Kenneth Williams]] in [[see:Round the Horne]].
In [[see:Polari]], a gay man.
A famous gay man, from the Polari passage Rob reads.
Polari for trousers, from [[see:lallies]], legs, and [[see:drag]]s, clothes.
Polari for legs.
Polari for clothes, which gives dressing up in drag; now celebrated and revived.
The everyday English phrase echoed by the Polari 'caught with her [[see:lally drags]] around her ankles'.
Polari for a public toilet where men meet for sex.
Polari for Piccadilly or Piccadilly Circus, also called the [[see:meat rack]].
Somewhere men go to strut; another name for [[see:the Dilly]].
Smart; used in Polari with the same meaning as Jack Sparrow's 'savvy'.
Can mean icy, or sometimes a gay man attracted to straight men.
Polari for eyeballs.
The general-purpose Polari word for good, handsome or beautiful.
The non-insulting Polari term for a gay man, literally man-woman, from [[from:omi]] and [[from:palone]].
Polari for man, one of the Italian-derived elements; part of [[gave:omi-palone]].
Polari for woman; part of [[gave:omi-palone]].
Polari for looking.
The Polari word for walking.
Polari for perfect, as in 'absolutely fantabulosa'.
Polari for hearing something.
What Polari speakers called their fathers, a protective way of avoiding saying something risky.
Polari for a drunkard.
A cant-like language of South African urban queer communities that, like [[see:Polari]], protects speakers from the law and ostracisation.
[[see:Michael Halliday]]'s 1970s term for a relexicalised form of a language arising within an [[see:anti-society]]; the hosts find it implies illegitimacy.
Linguist who wrote about [[see:anti-language]]s in the 1970s and set out criteria for them.
An intentionally separate community of ostracised people or those creating a separate social order, where an [[see:anti-language]] arises.
Using she for anyone is the one obvious grammatical change from [[see:Polari]], now revived and common in gay speech.
Words said backwards, or twisted backwards, documented by Hotten as the secret language of London [[see:costermongers]].
People selling food from hand carts, 30,000 to 40,000 of them in London according to Hotten, who spoke [[see:back slang]].
Back slang for crib, which came to mean a house.
Back slang for look.
Back slang for bad.
Back slang for bed.
Back slang for police, not reversed exactly because that would be too obvious.
Back slang for girl, used so she wouldn't know she was being talked about.
Back slang for woman.
Back slang for penny.
A twisted back slang form for a pound.
Grose defines it as the cant of thieves and gypsies, and a disguised language inserting a consonant between syllables, such as F gibberish.
Another name Grose gives for [[see:gibberish]], the cant of thieves and gypsies.
Another name Grose gives for [[see:gibberish]], the cant of thieves and gypsies.
